source: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Class X Political Science), Chapter 2

overview.bigIdea: Federalism is **vertical power sharing**: a government for the whole country and governments for the states (and in India, a third tier for villages and towns) – each with its own powers guaranteed by the constitution. India wrote it in the Constitution and made it work through **democratic politics**.

lessons.title: What is federalism?
lessons.hook: Picture two cooks sharing one kitchen: each has their own shelves, and neither can throw out the other’s ingredients. In a **federation**, the central government and the state governments each have their own powers – and neither can take them away from the other on its own.

core.def: A system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and various constituent units of the country.
Only one level of government, or sub-units subordinate to the central government, which can pass orders to them.
Independent states join to form a bigger unit – USA, Switzerland, Australia. States usually have equal power and are strong.
A large country divides power between states and the national government – India, Spain, Belgium. The Centre tends to be more powerful; units may have unequal powers.
Safeguard the unity of the country while accommodating regional diversity – needs mutual trust and agreement to live together.

explain: **Seven features:** (1) two or more tiers; (2) each tier governs the same citizens but has its own jurisdiction in legislation, taxation and administration; (3) jurisdictions specified in the constitution; (4) fundamental provisions cannot be changed by one level alone; (5) courts interpret the constitution and act as umpire; (6) sources of revenue clearly specified for financial autonomy; (7) dual objectives of unity and accommodating diversity.
Only 25 of the world’s 193 countries are federal, but they hold 40% of the world’s population. Belgium became federal in 1993; Sri Lanka remains, for all practical purposes, unitary.

example.q: What is the main difference between a federal and a unitary form of government? Explain with an example. (3 marks)
steps: **Federal:** power is divided between two or more levels, each with its own constitutional powers; the Centre cannot order a state to do something – e.g. India.
**Unitary:** there is one level of government, or sub-units are subordinate and receive orders from the Centre – e.g. Sri Lanka.
In a federation both levels are separately answerable to the people.
example.answer: Federal = constitutional powers for each level (India); unitary = sub-units subordinate (Sri Lanka).

mistakes: Putting India in ‘coming together’ – India is ‘holding together’.
Saying federalism needs a big country – Belgium is small but federal.
lessons.tip: In a 5-mark ‘features of federalism’ answer, write five of the seven features and add ‘e.g. India’ to at least two of them.
lessons.memory: Coming together = USA (States strong). Holding together = India (Centre strong).

lessons.title: What makes India a federal country?
lessons.hook: The Constitution never uses the word ‘federation’ – it calls India a **Union of States**. Yet every feature of federalism is there, starting with a neat idea: **three lists** that say who makes laws on what.

core.def: Subjects of national importance needing a uniform policy: defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications, currency. Only the Union makes laws.
Subjects of State and local importance: police, trade, commerce, agriculture, irrigation. Only the States make laws.
Common interest: education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption, succession. Both make laws; if they conflict, the Union law prevails.
Subjects in no list (e.g. computer software) – the Union Government legislates.
Assam, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram have special powers (Article 371). Union Territories (Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Delhi) have little power; the Centre runs them.

explain: Changing the power-sharing arrangement is hard: both Houses of Parliament must pass it with at least **two-thirds majority**, then legislatures of at least **half of the States** must ratify it.
The High Courts and Supreme Court settle disputes about the division of powers. Both Union and State governments can raise money through taxes.

example.q: Why is India called a federal country? Give three reasons. (3 marks)
steps: **Tiers:** there are three tiers – Union, State and local governments – each with its own jurisdiction.
**Three lists:** the Constitution divides legislative powers into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists; residuary powers are with the Union.
**Protected arrangement:** changes need a two-thirds majority in both Houses and ratification by half the States; courts settle disputes between levels.

mistakes: Putting education on the State List – it is Concurrent.
Saying the State law wins in a conflict on the Concurrent List.
Giving residuary powers to the States.
lessons.tip: Learn one ‘anchor’ subject per list: Defence (Union), Police (State), Education (Concurrent), Software (Residuary).

lessons.title: How is federalism practised?
lessons.hook: Rules on paper are not enough. Indian federalism succeeded because of **democratic politics**: the spirit of respecting diversity and the desire to live together. Three big tests show how.

core.def: Boundaries redrawn so that people speaking the same language live in one State. Feared to cause disintegration; actually made India more united and administration easier. Some States (Nagaland, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand) were created on culture, ethnicity or geography.

No national language. Hindi is the official language (mother tongue of only about 40–44%). 21 other Scheduled Languages (22 in all). English was to stop in 1965 but continued with Hindi after protests, violent in Tamil Nadu.

Earlier the same party ruled Centre and most States; the Centre often dismissed rival State governments. After 1990: rise of regional parties and coalition governments → new culture of respect for State autonomy.
A major judgement made it difficult for the Centre to dismiss State governments arbitrarily.

explain: Unlike Sri Lanka, Indian leaders took a **cautious attitude** in spreading Hindi. Promotion of Hindi is official policy, but it cannot be imposed on States that speak other languages.
The 2011 Census recorded more than 1300 mother tongues grouped into 121 major languages; 22 are Scheduled Languages.

example.q: How has federalism been strengthened in practice in India? (5 marks)
steps: **Linguistic States:** reorganising States by language made the country more united and administration easier.
**Other bases:** States like Nagaland, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand recognise differences of culture, ethnicity or geography.
**Language policy:** no national language; 22 Scheduled Languages; exams in any of them; English continued with Hindi after 1965 – avoiding a Sri Lanka-like conflict.
**Centre-State relations after 1990:** regional parties and coalition governments created respect for State autonomy.
**Judiciary:** a Supreme Court judgement made arbitrary dismissal of State governments difficult.
example.answer: Linguistic States + language policy + Centre-State relations + Supreme Court.

mistakes: Forgetting the role of coalition governments after 1990.
lessons.tip: Always contrast India with Sri Lanka in language questions – examiners reward the comparison.
lessons.memory: L-L-C: Linguistic States, Language policy, Centre-State relations.

lessons.title: Decentralisation in India
lessons.hook: Uttar Pradesh has more people than Russia! A State that big cannot be run only from its capital. So India added a **third tier**: panchayats and municipalities, where people solve local problems themselves.

core.def: Taking power away from the Central and State governments and giving it to local government.
Many problems are best settled locally; people know local problems and where to spend money; direct participation builds a habit of democratic participation – local self-government.
Regular elections compulsory · seats reserved for SC, ST and OBC · at least one-third for women · State Election Commission · States must share some powers and revenue.
Gram sabha (all voters) supervises the gram panchayat (panch + sarpanch) → panchayat samiti (block/mandal) → zilla parishad (chairperson).
Municipalities (chairperson) in towns; municipal corporations (mayor) in big cities.

explain: This is the **largest experiment in democracy** in the world: about 36 lakh elected representatives, and more than 10 lakh women representatives.
Problems remain: gram sabhas are not held regularly, and most States have not transferred significant powers or adequate resources.

example.q: State any two differences between local government before and after the 1992 amendment. (3 marks)
steps: **Elections:** before 1992 elections were not held regularly; now regular elections are constitutionally mandatory, conducted by the State Election Commission.
**Reservation:** now seats are reserved for SC, ST and OBC, and at least one-third for women.
**Powers:** earlier local bodies had no powers or resources of their own; now States must share some powers and revenue with them.
example.answer: Regular elections · reservations · powers and revenue.

mistakes: Saying one-half of seats are reserved for women (it is at least one-third).
Confusing gram sabha (all voters) with gram panchayat (elected council).
Calling the municipal corporation head the ‘chairperson’ (it is the mayor).
lessons.tip: Draw the panchayati raj ladder in your answer – a diagram earns marks and saves words.
lessons.memory: Sabha → Panchayat → Samiti → Parishad (village to district).

revision: Federalism: power divided between a central authority and constituent units; both levels separately answerable to the people.
Unitary: one level, or sub-units subordinate to the Centre (e.g. Sri Lanka). Belgium became federal in 1993.
Seven features: tiers, own jurisdiction, constitutional guarantee, joint consent for changes, courts as umpire, specified revenue, unity + diversity.
Coming together (USA, Switzerland, Australia) vs holding together (India, Spain, Belgium).

Union List (defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications, currency); State List (police, trade, commerce, agriculture, irrigation); Concurrent List (education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption, succession); residuary → Union.
Special status (Article 371): Assam, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram. UTs: Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Delhi.
Change needs two-thirds majority in both Houses + ratification by half the States.
Linguistic States made India more united; language policy: no national language, 22 Scheduled Languages, English continued.
After 1990: regional parties, coalitions, respect for State autonomy; Supreme Court limited arbitrary dismissals.
1992: regular elections, reservations (SC/ST/OBC, 1/3 women), State Election Commission, sharing powers and revenue.

sections.title: Federalism answers · 4 steps
items: Name the feature or change (e.g. ‘Three lists’).
Close with the purpose: unity with diversity / local self-government.

sections.title: Answer writing that scores
items: Start with a one-line definition or introduction using textbook keywords (e.g. ‘Majoritarianism is …’).
Write in points – one idea per point, with the key term in the first few words. A 3-mark answer needs 3 clear points; a 5-mark answer needs 5.
Add a real example from the chapter to each point (Belgium, Sri Lanka, Panchayati Raj, a party, a survey figure).
Use the exact numbers the textbook gives only when you are sure (59%, 1956, 1992, one-third, 1976).
For ‘Explain / Analyse’ questions use PEE: Point → Explain → Example. For ‘Distinguish’ questions draw a small two-column table.
Case-based questions: underline the key line in the passage first; the answer is usually hidden in it.

sections.title: Before the exam
items: Revise the key facts sheet and the revision list the night before.
Redo the Play & learn sorts – if you can sort every card first time, you know the chapter.
Practise one 5-mark answer in 8–10 minutes with a timer.

checklist: I can list five features of federalism.
I can explain coming together vs holding together with examples.
I can place any subject in the right list.
I can describe language policy and Centre-State relations after 1990.
I can list the changes of the 1992 amendment and draw the panchayati raj structure.
exam.paperNote: Based on the CBSE Class X Social Science pattern (MCQ, assertion–reason, 3-mark short, 4-mark case/source-based and 5-mark long answers). Practise these types first.

method: Built on proven learning methods: understand the story first, sort and match ideas with your hands (active learning), write model answers point by point, test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
